concept.body: The congruence test is a moving job: can some slide, turn, flip — or a chain of them — land figure 1 EXACTLY on figure 2? If yes, congruent. If any distance would have to stretch or shrink to make it fit, no motion exists and the figures are not congruent.

explanationVariants: Segments of lengths 4 and 4 match under a motion (slide one onto the other); lengths 4 and 5 never can — rigid motions can't stretch.
Equal lengths is exactly what lets a rigid motion do its job on segments.

widget.prompt: Segment GH has length 4. Which segment is guaranteed congruent to it?

options.label: a segment of length 4 anywhere in the plane
options.feedback: Slide (and turn, if needed) carries one length-4 segment onto any other — the motion exists, so they're congruent.

options.label: a segment of length 5 close by
options.feedback: Nearness doesn't help: a rigid motion would have to stretch 4 into 5, and rigid motions never stretch.

options.label: half of a segment of length 10
options.feedback: Half of 10 is 5, not 4 — one unit of stretch is still a stretch. Only length 4 matches length 4.

options.label: any segment on the same line as GH
options.feedback: Sharing a line says nothing about LENGTH — a length-9 segment on that line can never rigidly match a length-4 one.

steps.body: Here is the payoff of four chapters: **two figures are congruent exactly when some rigid motion (or chain of them) maps one precisely onto the other**. Not "they look alike" — a checkable claim: name a translation, rotation, reflection, or composition that carries every point of one onto the other.

widget.prompt: Which of these is NOT a rigid motion?

options.label: a dilation with scale factor 2
options.feedback: Doubling distances is exactly what rigid motions forbid — dilations change size, so they're out of the club.

options.label: a translation, sliding the figure sideways
options.feedback: A slide moves every point the same amount — gaps between points never change, so it's rigid.

options.label: a rotation about the center point
options.feedback: Turning a figure carries it around like a solid plate — every distance rides along unchanged: rigid.

options.label: a reflection across a mirror line
options.feedback: A mirror flips orientation but the image is the same size, point for point — reflections are rigid.

explanationVariants: ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF means precisely: some rigid motion maps ΔABC onto ΔDEF. Everything else (equal sides, equal angles) FOLLOWS from that.
The definition is existential — it promises a motion exists. To prove congruence, you exhibit the motion; to use congruence, you use what motions preserve.

options.label: some rigid motion maps ΔABC exactly onto ΔDEF
options.feedback: That's the definition — congruence is the existence of a distance-preserving motion between the figures.

options.label: the two triangles have the same area
options.feedback: Same area is far too weak — a 1×36 rectangle and a 6×6 square share area 36 and match nowhere. Congruence demands a point-for-point rigid match.

options.label: all three angles of one equal all three angles of the other
options.feedback: Equal angles alone is SIMILARITY — a triangle and its double have identical angles. Congruence also locks the size.

options.label: the triangles look identical when drawn carefully
options.feedback: "Looks identical" isn't checkable. The definition replaces the eyeball with an exhibit: name the motion that maps one onto the other.

steps.body: Why THIS definition works: rigid motions **preserve distance and angle measure**. So the instant a motion maps figure 1 onto figure 2, every side and every angle automatically matches — congruence of all the parts comes free, no measuring required.

widget.prompt: AB = 7. A rotation followed by a translation carries A to A′ and B to B′. What is A′B′?

commonErrors.feedback: Doubling is DILATION behavior. Rotations and translations are rigid — the gap between the two points rides along unchanged: 7.
Halving would shrink the figure — but rigid motions carry figures like solid plates. A′B′ = AB = 7.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Rigid motions preserve distance: A′B′ = AB = 7.

explanationVariants: Rigid motions preserve angle measure, so the image angle still measures 52°.
Reflections flip orientation — clockwise becomes counterclockwise — but the SIZE of the opening never changes: 52°.

widget.prompt: m∠P = 52°. A reflection maps ∠P to ∠P′. What is m∠P′ in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 128 is the SUPPLEMENT (180 − 52) — supplements come from straight-line pairs, not from motions. The mirror copies the opening exactly: 52°.
Halving the angle would distort the figure — reflections are rigid, so the measure is untouched: 52°.

steps.body: The club rules exclude dilations for a reason: a dilation with scale factor k multiplies EVERY distance by k. The image keeps the shape but not the size — that's **similarity**, a different (weaker) relationship. One stretched distance is enough to sink a congruence claim.

predict.prompt: Before you move the triangle, what should remain unchanged throughout any rigid motion?

options.label: Side lengths, but not angle measures

predict.reveal: The model can slide or reflect the triangle while every side length and angle measure stays fixed. Coordinates and orientation may change, but the figure's size and shape do not.

widget.prompt: Land the shape exactly on its target using a rigid motion — translate, and reflect if you need to. Watch the side lengths and the corner angles the whole way.
widget.successFeedback: It lands exactly, and nothing about the shape itself ever changed: every side kept its length and every corner kept its angle. That is what 'rigid' means — BOTH distances and angle measures survive, which is why congruent figures match part-for-part for free.
widget.offsetFeedback: Not on the target yet. Translation slides the shape without altering a single length or angle — keep moving it.
widget.reflectFeedback: A reflection flips the shape across the axis. Like translation it is rigid: the mirror image has identical side lengths and identical angles, just a reversed orientation.

hints: Apply the rule to each point: what are P′ and Q′?
P′ = (2, 4) and Q′ = (8, 4). How far apart are they?
Compare P′Q′ with PQ = 3 — what does a changed distance say about the motion?
explanationVariants: P(1,2) → (2,4), Q(4,2) → (8,4): P′Q′ = 8 − 2 = 6, double the original 3. Distance changed ⇒ the rule is not rigid ⇒ image and preimage are NOT congruent (they're similar).
The rule (2x, 2y) is a dilation, scale 2 — every distance doubles, so 3 becomes 6.

widget.prompt: P(1, 2) and Q(4, 2), so PQ = 3. Apply (x, y) → (2x, 2y) to both points. What is P′Q′?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 would mean the rule preserved distance — but (2x, 2y) is a dilation: P′ = (2, 4), Q′ = (8, 4), and the gap doubled to 6.
12 quadruples the distance — that would need scale factor 4. Doubling each coordinate doubles distances once: 2 × 3 = 6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: P′ = (2, 4), Q′ = (8, 4): P′Q′ = 6 — doubled, so not a rigid motion.

takeaways: Congruent = some rigid motion maps one figure exactly onto the other.
Rigid motions preserve distance AND angle — so all parts match for free.
Dilations change distances: same shape, different size — similarity, not congruence.
steps.teaser: Next: play detective — given the coordinates of both figures, NAME the motion that connects them.
